prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Three protesters scaled the Golden Gate Bridge Monday and unfurled a "Free Tibet" banner, a likely precursor to large protests when the Olympic torch arrives Wednesday in San Francisco, California. Members of Students for a Free Tibet climbed the bridge to place these banners, said the group's spokesman. The banner read, "One World. One Dream. Free Tibet." Those who climbed cables from which the bridge is suspended are members of Students for a Free Tibet, said group spokesman Tenzin Dasang. The three were arrested along with four others at the site. All seven were charged with felony conspiracy and misdemeanor nuisance, said California Highway Patrol Officer Mary Ziegenbein. The climbers also were charged with misdemeanor trespassing.  Watch protesters and banner hung from bridge » . The incident forced the closure of one northbound lane of the bridge. The climbers -- who were on the bridge for about three hours -- came down voluntarily about 1:15 p.m. (4:15 p.m. ET) after workers with the Golden Gate Bridge District began cutting down their banner, Ziegenbein said. Dasang said he has heard of many people planning to protest in San Francisco against China's human rights record. "We want it to be peaceful. But it will be large," said Dasang, 22, during a phone interview in which he said he was near the bridge. "I heard from Tibetans that now live all over the U.S. and even abroad who are coming here." The Olympic flame is on a 130-day journey that will take it through 23 cities on five continents and then throughout China, culminating at the Olympics opening ceremony in Beijing August 8. The San Francisco protest comes the same day as a demonstration in Paris, France, disrupted the torch relay many times. In Paris, police had to cut the Olympic torch relay short Monday amid protests against China's human rights record, French police said. The torch was scheduled to travel 17 miles, past Paris City Hall, but that stop and others were called off after the protests. The torch made it through about 10 miles of its scheduled journey. It was then driven by bus to its final destination, where it was displayed again during a public ceremony at a stadium. Authorities had to play hide-and-seek with the Olympic torch during much of the route, placing it on a bus at least twice during a sometimes chaotic relay route. China has come under international criticism because of its crackdown last month on protesters calling for democratic freedoms and self-rule in Tibet and neighboring Chinese provinces. Protesters have said more than 100 people have died in the crackdown, but Beijing denies that and has accused supporters of the Dalai Lama of orchestrating the violence. U.S. and other Western leaders have called on China to provide civil rights and freedoms to those in Tibet and to enter peaceful discussions aimed at resolving the crisis.  E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L1:
**(CNN) —** Three protesters scaled the Golden Gate Bridge on Monday and unfurled a “Free Tibet” banner, in what was likely a precursor to large demonstrations planned for the Olympic torch’s arrival Wednesday in San Francisco, California.

The protesters, members of Students for a Free Tibet, climbed the cables supporting the bridge to display banners, according to group spokesman Tenzin Dasang. One banner read, “One World. One Dream. Free Tibet.”

The three climbers were arrested along with four others at the site. All seven were charged with felony conspiracy and misdemeanor nuisance, California Highway Patrol Officer Mary Ziegenbein said. The climbers were also charged with misdemeanor trespassing.

*Watch protesters and banner hanging from bridge »*

The incident forced officials to close one northbound lane of the bridge. After spending about three hours on the structure, the climbers came down voluntarily at approximately 1:15 p.m. (4:15 p.m. ET), after workers with the Golden Gate Bridge District began cutting down their banner, Ziegenbein said.

Dasang said he had heard of many people planning to demonstrate in San Francisco against China’s human rights record.

“We want it to be peaceful. But it will be large,” Dasang, 22, said during a phone interview from near the bridge. “I heard from Tibetans that now live all over the U.S. and even abroad who are coming here.”

The Olympic flame is on a 130-day journey through 23 cities on five continents, followed by a tour throughout China. The relay will culminate at the opening ceremony of the Beijing Olympics on August 8.

The San Francisco protest came on the same day that a demonstration in Paris, France, repeatedly disrupted the torch relay. French police said they had to cut the relay short Monday amid protests over China’s human rights record.

The torch had been scheduled to travel 17 miles, passing Paris City Hall, but that stop and others were canceled because of the demonstrations. It completed approximately 10 miles of the planned route before being transported by bus to its final destination, where it was displayed again during a public ceremony at a stadium.

Authorities were forced to play hide-and-seek with the Olympic torch along much of the route, placing it on a bus at least twice during the sometimes-chaotic relay.

China has faced international criticism over its crackdown last month on protesters calling for democratic freedoms and self-rule in Tibet and neighboring Chinese provinces. Protesters have said that more than 100 people died in the crackdown, but Beijing denies the claim and has accused supporters of the Dalai Lama of orchestrating the violence.

U.S. and other Western leaders have called on China to grant civil rights and freedoms to people in Tibet and to enter into peaceful discussions aimed at resolving the crisis.

outputs.L2:
Three demonstrators climbed the Golden Gate Bridge on Monday and displayed a banner calling for a “Free Tibet,” an action that may signal larger protests when the Olympic torch reaches San Francisco, California, on Wednesday.

Tenzin Dasang, a spokesperson for Students for a Free Tibet, said members of the organization climbed the bridge’s suspension cables to hang banners. One carried the message: “One World. One Dream. Free Tibet.”

Police arrested the three climbers and four other people at the scene. California Highway Patrol Officer Mary Ziegenbein said all seven faced a felony conspiracy charge and a misdemeanor nuisance charge. The climbers were additionally charged with misdemeanor trespassing.

The protest caused officials to close one northbound lane. After remaining on the bridge for roughly three hours, the climbers voluntarily descended at about 1:15 p.m. local time, or 4:15 p.m. ET. Ziegenbein said they came down after Golden Gate Bridge District workers began removing the banner.

Dasang, 22, said by phone from near the bridge that he had learned of many people intending to demonstrate in San Francisco over China’s human rights record.

“We want it to be peaceful. But it will be large,” he said, adding that Tibetans living across the United States and even overseas planned to travel to the city.

The Olympic flame was in the midst of a 130-day tour spanning 23 cities on five continents before continuing through China. Its journey was scheduled to conclude at the Beijing Olympics’ opening ceremony on August 8.

The San Francisco action occurred on the same day that protests in Paris, France, repeatedly interrupted the torch relay. French police said the demonstrations, which also focused on China’s human rights record, forced authorities to end Monday’s relay early.

The original Paris route covered 17 miles and was to pass City Hall, but that appearance and several other stops were canceled. The flame completed about 10 miles before being transported by bus to the final venue, where it was once again presented during a public ceremony at a stadium.

For much of the route, authorities were effectively forced to conceal and relocate the torch amid the disorder, putting it aboard a bus on at least two occasions.

China had drawn international condemnation following its crackdown the previous month on protesters demanding democratic rights and Tibetan self-government in Tibet and nearby Chinese provinces. Demonstrators claimed that more than 100 people were killed, an assertion Beijing rejected. Chinese officials instead accused Dalai Lama supporters of organizing the violence.

Leaders in the United States and other Western countries urged China to guarantee civil rights and freedoms for Tibetans and to begin peaceful negotiations intended to resolve the crisis.
